title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Continuous Batching
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 11)
Understanding Continuous Batching
In the previous part, we explored one of the most important runtime ideas in inference systems:

Prefill
vs
Decode

Prefill is highly parallel. Decode is sequential. During prefill, the model processes many prompt tokens together. This creates large matrix operations and keeps GPUs busy. But during decode, the model generates one token at a time. That creates a very different problem. Even if we have powerful GPUs, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, replicas, and high-speed networking, the system can still struggle because decode does not naturally give the GPU enough work. So the next question becomes:

How do modern inference systems
keep GPUs busy during decode?
This leads us to:
Continuous Batching
Continuous batching is one of the key ideas behind modern LLM serving systems.
Why do we need batching again?
Before understanding continuous batching, let us quickly revisit batching. Suppose one user sends a request:
Request A
If we run only this one request on a GPU, the GPU may not be fully utilized. So instead, the system groups multiple requests together. Example:
Batch = [Request A, Request B, Request C, Request D]
Now the GPU processes them together. This improves throughput because GPUs are much better at handling larger parallel workloads. So batching helps us turn:
many small jobs
into:
one larger GPU job
What is traditional batching?
In traditional batching, the system waits for a group of requests. Example:

Request A
Request B
Request C
Request D
Then it forms a batch:
Batch 1 = [A, B, C, D]
Then the system runs this batch. The simple mental model is:

collect requests
run batch
finish batch
start next batch
This works reasonably well when all requests are similar. But LLM inference requests are not similar.
Why are LLM requests different?
In LLM inference, every request can be different. One user may send a short prompt:
"Summarize this paragraph"
Another user may send a long prompt:
"Analyze this long document"
One user may ask for a short answer. Another user may ask for a long explanation. So requests differ in:

prompt length
output length
arrival time
stopping point
memory usage
This makes batching much harder.
What goes wrong with traditional batching?
Suppose we create a batch like this:
Batch = [A, B, C, D]

Now each request starts generating tokens. But maybe Request A only needs 5 output tokens. Request B needs 20 output tokens. Request C needs 50 output tokens. Request D needs 100 output tokens. So they finish at different times. Example:

A finishes early
B finishes later
C keeps going
D keeps going much longer
Now what should the system do? In a naive batching system, the batch may stay tied together until the slowest request finishes. That means some slots become wasted.
What does a wasted slot mean?
Imagine the batch has 4 slots:
[A, B, C, D]
After some decode steps, Request A finishes. Now the batch looks like:
[empty, B, C, D]
The system is still running decode steps. But one slot is empty. Later, Request B finishes:
[empty, empty, C, D]
Now half the batch is empty. The GPU is still doing work, but less efficiently. This is the core problem. Static batches become less useful as requests finish at different times.
Why is this especially bad during decode?
Decode already has small workloads because generation happens one token at a time. So if the batch also becomes smaller over time, the problem becomes worse. The system now has:

small decode work
+
shrinking batch
That is bad for GPU utilization. The GPU wants large parallel work. But decode gives it small sequential work. And static batching makes that work shrink even more. The batch starts full:
[A, B, C, D]
Then becomes:
[empty, B, C, D]
Then:
[empty, empty, C, D]
Then:
[empty, empty, empty, D]
At the end, we are almost back to serving one request. That is exactly what batching was supposed to avoid.
What does continuous batching change?

Continuous batching changes the batch while generation is happening. Instead of waiting for the entire batch to finish, the scheduler updates the batch continuously. When one request finishes, it leaves. When a new request is waiting, it enters. So the batch is not fixed. It is dynamic.
What does that look like?
Suppose we start with:
Batch = [A, B, C, D]
After a few decode steps, Request A finishes. Instead of leaving that slot empty, the scheduler inserts a new request.
Batch = [E, B, C, D]
Later, Request B finishes. Another request enters.
Batch = [E, F, C, D]
Then Request C finishes.
Batch = [E, F, G, D]
So the batch keeps changing. The GPU keeps receiving useful work. That is continuous batching.
What is the key idea?
Traditional batching works like this:

create batch
run until batch is done
start next batch
Continuous batching works like this:

run one decode step
remove finished requests
add waiting requests
run next decode step
repeat
The batch is updated during generation. This is why continuous batching is also often described as:
iteration-level scheduling
Because the scheduler makes decisions at the level of each generation step.
What is a decode iteration?
A decode iteration is one step of token generation. For active requests, the model generates the next token. Example:

Step 1 → generate next token
Step 2 → generate next token
Step 3 → generate next token
Each step updates the KV cache and produces the next token for each active request. With continuous batching, the scheduler can adjust the active batch between these steps.
What does the scheduler do?
The scheduler constantly decides:

Which requests should run now?
Which requests are finished?
Which new requests can enter?
Is there enough KV cache memory?
How large should the active batch be?
So the scheduler is not just forming batches once. It is managing the batch continuously. This is why modern inference systems are deeply scheduler-driven.
Why not just run every request immediately?

At first, it may seem like the best system should run every request as soon as it arrives. But this creates another problem. If the system runs very small batches immediately, throughput decreases. Why? Because every decode step has overhead. The system still needs to:

launch GPU work
read model weights
read KV cache
run attention
run matrix operations
synchronize GPUs
write updated KV cache
If the batch is very small, all of that overhead is paid for only a few tokens. Example:
Batch = [A]
The GPU is doing a full decode step, but only one request gets one token. Now compare that with:
Batch = [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H]

The system still runs a decode step, but now many requests each receive a token. So the overhead is spread across more useful work. That is why very small batches often have poor throughput. The GPU may be active, but not efficiently used.
What does throughput mean here?
Throughput means how much useful work the system completes over time. For LLM serving, this is often measured as:
tokens per second

If the system runs one tiny batch immediately, latency for that one request may look good. But total tokens per second may be low. If the system waits a little and forms a larger batch, total tokens per second may improve. But users may wait longer before their request starts. So the system is constantly balancing:

latency
vs
throughput
Why does batching improve throughput?

Batching improves throughput because GPUs are designed for parallel computation. A GPU does not want to do a tiny amount of work. It wants large tensor operations. With a larger batch, the GPU can process more tokens together. That usually means:

better GPU utilization
more tokens per second
lower cost per token
But the system cannot wait forever to build a large batch. If it waits too long, user latency becomes bad. So the scheduler must find a balance.
What is the latency-throughput tradeoff?
If the scheduler runs requests immediately:

low waiting time
small batch
lower throughput
If the scheduler waits to collect more requests:

larger batch
higher throughput
more waiting time

Continuous batching helps because new requests do not always need to wait for a full old batch to finish. They can enter between decode steps. So continuous batching gives the system a better way to balance:

keep users moving
while also keeping GPUs busy
Does continuous batching reduce latency?

It can help, but it is not magic. Continuous batching can reduce unnecessary waiting because new requests may enter as soon as there is room. In a traditional system, a new request might wait until the entire current batch finishes. Example:

Current batch still running
New request waits
With continuous batching:

Decode step finishes
Request A leaves
Request E enters
Next decode step begins

This can reduce queueing delay. But the scheduler still needs to be careful. If it admits too many requests, active users may slow down. If it admits too few requests, GPU utilization may drop. So continuous batching improves flexibility, but scheduling is still a tradeoff.
Does every new request enter immediately?
Not always. The scheduler still considers:

available KV cache
current batch size
prompt length
decode workload
latency targets
fairness

A long prompt may require expensive prefill before it can join decode. A short request may be easier to admit. A system may also limit how many new requests enter at once to avoid hurting active users. So continuous batching is not simply:
add every request immediately
It is more like:

carefully admit requests
while keeping the system efficient
How does prefill interact with continuous batching?
A new request usually starts with prefill. The prompt must be processed first. Only after prefill does the request enter the decode loop. So there are two kinds of work:

prefill work
decode work

Prefill can be large and compute-heavy. Decode is smaller and repeated many times. A scheduler must decide how to mix them. If too much prefill is admitted at once, active decode requests may slow down. If decode is always prioritized, new requests may wait too long before their first token. So the scheduler must balance:

time to first token
vs
ongoing token generation speed
What is time to first token?
Time to first token means:

how long the user waits
before seeing the first generated token

This depends heavily on prefill. If the prompt is long, prefill takes longer. If the system queue is busy, the request waits longer. So continuous batching is not only about total throughput. It also affects perceived responsiveness.
What is token generation latency?
After the first token appears, the user cares about how quickly the remaining tokens stream. This is related to decode speed. So there are two user-facing latency experiences:
waiting for the first token
and:
waiting between generated tokens

Continuous batching affects both. If the scheduler is too aggressive, each request may wait longer between decode steps. If it is too conservative, GPU utilization may drop. This is why scheduling is such an important part of inference systems.
Why does KV cache matter here?

Every active request needs KV cache. When a request enters the batch, the system must allocate KV cache memory for it. When a request finishes, its KV cache can be freed. So continuous batching is not just about compute. It is also about memory management. The scheduler cannot simply add unlimited requests. It must check:

Do we have enough KV cache space?
Can this request fit?
How many tokens might it generate?
Will adding this request hurt latency?
This is where continuous batching starts connecting directly to paged attention.
Why does continuous batching make memory harder?
Because requests are constantly entering and leaving. That means KV cache memory is constantly changing. Example:

Request A enters → allocate KV cache
Request B enters → allocate KV cache
Request A finishes → free KV cache
Request C enters → allocate KV cache
Request D grows → allocate more KV cache
This creates a dynamic memory problem. The system needs to manage many growing and shrinking sequences efficiently. If memory management is poor, we get:

fragmentation
wasted memory
failed allocations
lower batch size
lower throughput
So continuous batching improves GPU utilization, but it also increases the importance of KV cache management.
Why does this lead to PagedAttention?

Once batches become dynamic, KV cache memory becomes harder to manage. Requests have different lengths. They grow token by token. They finish at different times. Their memory needs change continuously. So the system needs a smarter way to store and reuse KV cache memory. This is where PagedAttention becomes important. The rough connection is:

Continuous batching
keeps the GPU busy

PagedAttention
helps manage KV cache memory efficiently
while batches change dynamically
That is why these two ideas often appear together in modern serving systems.
How does continuous batching help decode?
Decode is inefficient because each request generates only one token at a time. But if we have many active requests, we can decode one token for many requests together. Example:

A → next token
B → next token
C → next token
D → next token
This gives the GPU more useful work. Continuous batching tries to keep this active set full. So instead of decode looking like:
one request generating one token
it becomes:
many requests generating one token each
This is much better for throughput.
What does this look like inside a serving system?
At a high level:

Waiting Queue
    ↓
Scheduler
    ↓
Active Batch
    ↓
GPU Decode Step
    ↓
Finished requests leave
    ↓
New requests enter
    ↓
Repeat
The active batch is constantly changing. The scheduler keeps checking:

Who is waiting?
Who is active?
Who finished?
Who needs memory?
Who should run next?
This loop is the heart of continuous batching.
How is this different from normal backend batching?
In normal backend systems, batching often means:

collect similar requests
process them together
return results
But LLM generation is different because requests are long-running. A request does not finish after one forward pass. It may need:

10 decode steps
50 decode steps
500 decode steps
So batching must happen across time. That is the key difference. Continuous batching is designed for long-running generation.
What is the simplest intuition?
Imagine a bus. Traditional batching is like:

fill the bus
drive until every passenger reaches their destination
only then pick up new passengers
That is inefficient. Some passengers get off early, but their seats stay empty. Continuous batching is like:

passengers get off at each stop
new passengers get on
the bus keeps moving
The bus stays full more often. That is the intuition.
What is the GPU version of this?
The GPU does not want empty seats. The batch is the bus. Requests are passengers. Finished requests leave. New requests enter. The scheduler keeps the bus full. That is continuous batching.
What problem does it solve?
Continuous batching mainly helps solve:
decode underutilization
During decode, each request gives only a small amount of work. So the system needs many active requests to keep the GPU busy. Continuous batching helps maintain that active set.
What problem does it not solve?

Continuous batching does not remove the sequential nature of generation. The model still generates one token at a time. Token 2 still depends on token 1. Token 3 still depends on token 2. So continuous batching does not make one request magically parallel across future tokens. Instead, it improves system-level efficiency by batching many users together. The key distinction is:

Single request generation is still sequential.

Many requests can be scheduled together efficiently.
How does this connect to replicas?
Each replica usually has its own scheduler. Example:

Replica 1 → Scheduler 1 → Active batch
Replica 2 → Scheduler 2 → Active batch
Replica 3 → Scheduler 3 → Active batch

The router sends requests to replicas. Then each replica manages its own continuous batching loop. This means batching happens inside each serving replica. The router balances traffic across replicas. The scheduler balances work inside a replica.
Why can’t we freely move requests between replicas?

Because each request has KV cache stored inside its assigned replica. If a request moves to another replica, its KV cache would also need to move. That is expensive. So once a request starts generating, it usually stays on the same replica. This is why earlier we talked about:

sticky sessions
or
session affinity
Continuous batching works within that constraint.
What does continuous batching optimize for?
It tries to improve:

GPU utilization
throughput
queue waiting time
decode efficiency
batch occupancy
But it must also protect:

latency
fairness
memory safety
user experience
So the scheduler is constantly making tradeoffs.
Why is this harder than it sounds?

Because every request is different. Some requests have long prompts. Some have short prompts. Some generate short outputs. Some generate very long outputs. Some arrive during quiet periods. Some arrive during traffic spikes. Some need streaming responses. Some may stop early. Some may hit max token limits. So the scheduler is managing a moving target. There is no single fixed batch. There is only a constantly changing set of active sequences.
What is the key mental model?
Traditional batching:

Batch is fixed.
Requests enter together.
Requests leave together.
Continuous batching:

Batch is dynamic.
Requests enter when there is room.
Requests leave when they finish.
That is the core idea.
Why is continuous batching so important?

Because decode is where inference systems often struggle. Prefill gives the GPU large parallel work. Decode gives the GPU small repeated work. Continuous batching helps convert many small decode steps into one larger repeated workload. So instead of thinking:
one user generating tokens
we should think:
many users advancing one token at a time together
That is much closer to how modern serving systems keep GPUs busy.
What does this teach us about inference systems?
At this point, inference starts looking less like a simple model call. It looks more like a runtime scheduling problem. The system is constantly asking:

Which requests should run now?
How much memory do they need?
How do we keep the GPU busy?
How do we avoid making users wait too long?
How do we handle requests finishing at different times?
This is why scheduler design is such a central part of modern LLM serving.
What comes next?

Now we understand why continuous batching matters. It keeps the active batch full during decode by allowing requests to enter and leave dynamically. But this creates another major problem. If requests are constantly entering, growing, and leaving, then KV cache memory becomes difficult to manage efficiently. The system needs a way to store KV cache without wasting huge amounts of GPU memory. That leads directly to one of the most important ideas in vLLM:
PagedAttention
In the next part, we will explore:

why KV cache memory becomes fragmented
why fixed allocation wastes memory
how paging helps
why PagedAttention is similar to virtual memory
how it works together with continuous batching
Because continuous batching keeps the compute side busy. PagedAttention helps make the memory side efficient.
